docs.text: PyTorch in One Hour — Study Notes Personal study notes based on "PyTorch in One Hour: From Tensors to Training Neural Networks on Multiple GPUs" by Sebastian Raschka (Jul 2025). Original tutorial: https://sebastianraschka.com/teaching/pytorch-1h/ These notes summarize the concepts in my own words; read the original for full explanations, figures, and outputs. Contents What PyTorch is Tensors Computation graphs Autograd Building models with nn.Module Datasets & DataLoaders The training loop Saving & loading GPUs: single and multi-GPU (DDP) Quick reference & gotchas Further reading 1. What PyTorch Is Three core components: Component What it gives you Tensor library NumPy-like arrays that can run on CPU or GPU Autograd engine Automatic gradient computation for backpropagation Deep learning utilities Layers, loss functions, optimizers, data loading Terminology hierarchy: AI ⊃ Machine Learning ⊃ Deep Learning (deep neural nets) — LLMs live inside deep learning. Supervised learning workflow: train on labeled data → evaluate → predict labels for new data. Installation tips Use a Python version 1–2 releases behind the latest (better library support). pip install torch — or use the selector at pytorch.org for a specific CUDA build. Sanity checks: torch.__version__ torch.cuda.is_available() → NVIDIA GPU torch.backends.mps.is_available() → Apple Silicon No GPU? Google Colab offers free, time-limited GPU runtimes. 2. Tensors A tensor generalizes scalars/vectors/matrices to N dimensions. Rank 0 = scalar, rank 1 = vector, rank 2 = matrix, rank 3+ = "3D tensor", etc. Think of them as data containers with GPU support + gradient tracking. Creating tensors import torch s = torch.tensor(7) # 0D v = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3]) # 1D m = torch.tensor([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) # 2D Data types Python ints → torch.int64 Python floats → torch.float32 (default; good precision/speed trade-off, GPU-optimized) Convert with .to() : v_float = v.to(torch.float32) Essential operations Operation Purpose .shape Dimensions .reshape(r, c) / .view(r, c) Change shape ( .view is very common) .T Transpose (not the same as reshape!) a.matmul(b) or a @ b Matrix multiplication Why duplicate APIs? PyTorch inherited Lua Torch conventions, then added NumPy-style aliases. 3. Models as Computation Graphs A computation graph is a directed graph of the operations that produce an output (and loss). PyTorch builds this graph dynamically in the background as you run operations. The graph is what makes gradient computation possible. Example idea — logistic regression forward pass: input × weight + bias → sigmoid → compare with label → loss 4. Autograd (Automatic Differentiation) Set requires_grad=True on parameters you want gradients for. Backpropagation = applying the chain rule from the loss backward through the graph. Two ways to get gradients import torch.nn.functional as F w = torch.tensor([1.5], requires_grad=True) b = torch.tensor([0.0], requires_grad=True) x, y = torch.tensor([2.0]), torch.tensor([1.0]) loss = F.binary_cross_entropy(torch.sigmoid(x * w + b), y) # Option A: manual (debugging / experiments) # from torch.autograd import grad # dw = grad(loss, w, retain_graph=True) # Option B: the usual way loss.backward() print(w.grad, b.grad) Key points - The graph is freed after computing gradients unless retain_graph=True . - .backward() fills .grad on all leaf tensors. - Takeaway: you rarely compute derivatives by hand — PyTorch does the calculus. 5. Building Neural Networks with nn.Module Pattern Subclass torch.nn.Module Define layers in __init__ Define data flow in forward backward is generated automatically class MLP(torch.nn.Module): def __init__(self, n_in, n_out): super().__init__() self.net = torch.nn.Sequential( torch.nn.Linear(n_in, 32), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(32, 16), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(16, n_out), # outputs raw logits ) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) Useful inspections print(model) — architecture summary Count trainable params: python sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad) Access a layer's weights: model.net[0].weight , .bias , .shape Concepts worth remembering nn.Linear = weight matrix multiply + bias ("fully connected" / "feedforward" layer). Random init breaks symmetry so neurons learn different things. Reproducibility: torch.manual_seed(123) before creating the model. grad_fn on an output (e.g. AddmmBackward0 ) shows the last op recorded in the graph. Inference best practices Wrap prediction in torch.no_grad() → saves memory & compute. Models return logits (no softmax) because loss functions like cross_entropy apply softmax internally for numerical stability. Want probabilities? Call torch.softmax(logits, dim=1) explicitly. 6. Efficient Data Loading Two classes: - Dataset — how to fetch one example - DataLoader — shuffling, batching, parallel loading Custom Dataset: three required methods Method Role __init__ Store data / paths / connections __getitem__(i) Return one (features, label) pair __len__ Number of examples from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader class MyDataset(Dataset): def __init__(self, X, y): self.X, self.y = X, y def __getitem__(self, i): return self.X[i], self.y[i] def __len__(self): return len(self.y) loader = DataLoader(MyDataset(X, y), batch_size=32, shuffle=True, drop_last=True, num_workers=4) DataLoader settings cheat sheet Setting Guidance shuffle=True For training; order changes each epoch (avoids repetitive update cycles) shuffle=False For validation/test drop_last=True Drops a small final batch that can hurt convergence num_workers=0 Loads in main process — can starve the GPU on big jobs num_workers>0 Parallel loading; ~4 is often a good start. Avoid in Jupyter / tiny datasets Class labels must start at 0 and go up to num_output_nodes - 1 . Epoch = one full pass over the training set. 7. A Typical Training Loop model = MLP(n_in=2, n_out=2) optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.5) for epoch in range(num_epochs): model.train() for features, labels in train_loader: logits = model(features) loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels) optimizer.zero_grad() # 1. clear old gradients loss.backward() # 2. compute new gradients optimizer.step() # 3. update parameters model.eval() # evaluate on validation data here The core three-step rhythm optimizer.zero_grad() — don't forget , or gradients accumulate loss.backward() optimizer.step() Train vs eval mode model.train() / model.eval() matter for dropout and batch norm . Include them always — protects you when the architecture changes later. Hyperparameters & data splits Learning rate and number of epochs are hyperparameters — tuned by watching the loss. Validation set: used many times to tune hyperparameters. Test set: use once, at the end, for an unbiased estimate. From logits to predictions torch.argmax(logits, dim=1) → predicted class (softmax not required for argmax). Accuracy = (preds == labels).sum() / len(labels) . For large data, compute accuracy batch-by-batch through a DataLoader: def accuracy(model, loader): model.eval() correct, total = 0, 0 with torch.no_grad(): for x, y in loader: preds = model(x).argmax(dim=1) correct += (preds == y).sum().item() total += y.size(0) return correct / total 8. Saving & Loading Models Recommended: save the state_dict (parameter dictionary), not the whole object. # Save torch.save(model.state_dict(), "model.pth") # Load model = MLP(2, 2) # architecture must match exactly model.load_state_dict(torch.load("model.pth", weights_only=True)) .pth / .pt are conventional extensions. You need a model instance in memory before loading weights. 9. Training on GPUs 9.1 Device basics A device is where tensors live and ops run ( "cpu" , "cuda" , "cuda:1" , "mps" ). Move with .to(device) . All tensors in an operation must be on the same device — otherwise RuntimeError . 9.2 Single-GPU training — only 3 changes device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") # Apple Silicon: "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" model.to(device) # change 1 & 2 for features, labels in train_loader: features, labels = features.to(device), labels.to(device) # change 3 ... Tiny models may not speed up (transfer overhead); big models / LLMs benefit hugely. 9.3 Multi-GPU with DistributedDataParallel (DDP) How DDP works 1. One process per GPU, each with a full model copy . 2. DistributedSampler gives each GPU a different, non-overlapping slice of data. 3. Each GPU runs forward + backward independently. 4. Gradients are averaged and synced across GPUs → all copies stay identical. 5. Result: near-linear speedup (2 GPUs ≈ 2× faster per epoch, minus communication overhead). Key building blocks | Piece | Role | |---|---| | init_process_group(backend=...) | Start distributed communication ( nccl on Linux/NVIDIA, gloo on Windows) | | torch.cuda.set_device(rank) | Pin each process to its GPU | | DistributedSampler(dataset) | Split data across processes (set shuffle=False on the DataLoader) | | DDP(model, device_ids=[rank]) | Wrap the model; original is at model.module | | sampler.set_epoch(epoch) | Different shuffle order each epoch | | destroy_process_group() | Clean shutdown | Skeleton import os from torch.utils.data.distributed import DistributedSampler from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP from torch.distributed import init_process_group, destroy_process_group def main(rank, world_size): os.environ.setdefault("MASTER_ADDR", "localhost") os.environ.setdefault("MASTER_PORT", "12355") init_process_group("nccl", rank=rank, world_size=world_size) torch.cuda.set_device(rank) loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, shuffle=False, sampler=DistributedSampler(ds), pin_memory=True) model = DDP(MLP(2, 2).to(rank), device_ids=[rank]) # ... standard training loop, calling loader.sampler.set_epoch(epoch) ... destroy_process_group() if __name__ == "__main__": world_size = int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", 1)) rank = int(os.environ.get("LOCAL_RANK", 0)) main(rank, world_size) Launching with torchrun (handles process spawning + env vars like RANK , LOCAL_RANK , WORLD_SIZE ): torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 train_ddp.py torchrun --nproc_per_node=$(nvidia-smi -L | wc -l) train_ddp.py # all GPUs DDP gotchas - ❌ Doesn't work in Jupyter — run as a script. - Duplicate log lines → each process prints. Guard with if rank == 0: . - Tiny datasets may leave some GPUs with zero batches → enlarge data for more GPUs. - Model too big for one GPU? Look at FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel). 10. Quick Reference & Gotchas Checklist for any training script - [ ] torch.manual_seed(...) for reproducibility - [ ] Model returns logits; use F.cross_entropy - [ ] optimizer.zero_grad() → loss.backward() → optimizer.step() - [ ] model.train() / model.eval() toggled appropriately - [ ] torch.no_grad() for inference/evaluation - [ ] Model and data on the same device - [ ] Save with state_dict() Common errors | Symptom | Likely cause | |---|---| | "Expected all tensors to be on the same device" | Forgot .to(device) on data or model | | Loss explodes / weird training | Missing zero_grad() (gradient accumulation) | | Label index errors in loss | Labels not in 0 … num_classes-1 | | Notebook crash with DataLoader | num_workers > 0 in Jupyter | | Slow GPU training | Data loading bottleneck → raise num_workers | Why isn't zero_grad() automatic? Because sometimes you want to accumulate gradients (e.g., gradient accumulation to simulate larger batches on limited memory). 11. Further Reading (from the tutorial) Machine Learning with PyTorch and Scikit-Learn — Raschka, Liu, Mirjalili (2022) Deep Learning with PyTorch — Stevens, Antiga, Viehmann (2021) Video: Tensors in Deep Learning — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JXfDlgrfOBY Model Evaluation, Selection & Algorithm Selection — https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.12808 Introduction to Calculus (free PDF) — https://sebastianraschka.com/pdf/supplementary/calculus.pdf Gradient accumulation for LLM finetuning — https://sebastianraschka.com/blog/2023/llm-grad-accumulation.html PyTorch FSDP intro — https://pytorch.org/blog/introducing-pytorch-fully-sharded-data-parallel-api/ DDP API docs — https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.html
